chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala, from Al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Muskhan, from 'Umar ibn Hanathala, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I am your ransom, I asked you about making up the daytime prayers at night while traveling, and you said, "Do not make them up." And our companions asked you, and you said, "Make them up." He said to me, "So should I tell them, "Do not pray," while I dislike telling them, "Do not pray," and by God, that is not the case for them."'

As for the report narrated by Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hanan ibn Sadir from Sadir, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'My father used to make up the daytime supererogatory prayers at night while traveling, and he did not complete a mandatory prayer.'

So it is possible that the meaning of this report is what we mentioned in the first report, and it is also possible that he (peace be upon him) only made up these supererogatory prayers if he set out for travel after their time had entered. This possibility is also supported by the first report, that whoever ordered him to make up the supererogatory prayers knew from his state that he had set out after the time had entered, and whoever ordered him to leave them knew from his state that he had set out after the time had passed, and that is what indicates it.
ai.seo_question: When should daytime supererogatory prayers be made up at night while traveling?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* resolves the apparent contradiction in Imam al-Sadiq’s (AS) rulings on making up daytime *nafl* prayers while traveling by introducing the concept of *taqiyya* (dissimulation) and contextual timing. The Imam’s varying commands—'do not make them up' versus 'make them up'—were tailored to the specific circumstances of his companions, specifically whether they departed before or after the prayer time had entered, demonstrating the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in adapting to practical realities.
